# fpcloud_firewall (Resource)

Manages a firewall: a project's ordered access list on client addresses, enforced at the platform's edge. Rules are evaluated in priority order, lowest first, the first match decides, and a request no rule matches gets `default_action`. A firewall does nothing until it is attached: set `firewall` on an fpcloud_app or on an fpcloud_bucket serving a website, and it applies to every host the edge serves for that target, custom domains included. It covers requests arriving through the edge and nothing else: not calls between apps inside the platform, and not outbound traffic. The rules declared here are the whole list: a rule added outside this configuration is removed by the next apply. A rule matches the address the edge sees the connection come from, so behind a CDN or a proxy of your own the rules see that CDN's addresses, never the visitor's.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# An allowlist: only the office and the VPN reach the app. Rules are evaluated
# in priority order, lowest first, and a request no rule matches gets
# default_action.
resource "fpcloud_firewall" "office" {
  project        = fpcloud_project.production.id
  name           = "office"
  description    = "The office and the VPN, nobody else"
  default_action = "deny"

  rules = [
    {
      priority    = 100
      action      = "allow"
      description = "Office"
      match = {
        sources = ["198.51.100.0/24", "2001:db8:100::/48"]
      }
    },
    {
      priority    = 200
      action      = "allow"
      description = "VPN exit"
      match = {
        sources = ["203.0.113.7"] # a bare address is the one-address range
      }
    },
  ]
}

# The firewall does nothing until something names it. It then applies to every
# host the edge serves for the app, custom domains included.
resource "fpcloud_app" "admin" {
  project_id = fpcloud_project.production.id
  name       = "admin"
  image      = "ghcr.io/myorg/admin:latest"
  ingress    = "all"

  firewall = fpcloud_firewall.office.id
}

# A blocklist is the other way round: everyone is let in but the listed ranges.
resource "fpcloud_firewall" "blocklist" {
  project = fpcloud_project.production.id
  name    = "blocklist"

  rules = [
    {
      priority = 100
      action   = "deny"
      match = {
        sources = ["192.0.2.0/24"]
      }
    },
  ]
}

# The same attribute attaches one to a bucket's website.
resource "fpcloud_bucket" "docs" {
  project         = fpcloud_project.production.id
  name            = "docs"
  website_enabled = true
  firewall        = fpcloud_firewall.blocklist.id
}
```

## Behind a CDN of your own

A rule matches the address the platform's edge sees the connection come from.
When a CDN or a proxy of your own sits in front of the app, that is the CDN's
address: every visitor arrives from the CDN's ranges, and the visitor's own
address is in a header the firewall does not read. Two things follow.

- An allowlist of office addresses lets nobody in, because no request arrives
  from the office.
- An allowlist of the CDN's published ranges does work, and is the usual use:
  it closes the app to anyone who goes around the CDN to the platform host.
  Filtering by visitor is then the CDN's job.

## What an apply waits for

A change is stored at once and enforced by the edge shortly after. An apply
that changes a firewall's rules or default action returns once every app and
website it is attached to enforces the new revision, and one that sets, changes
or removes `firewall` on an app or a bucket returns once the edge enforces the
result. It waits five minutes at most and fails with the edge's own reason if
the edge refuses the change.

A firewall that is still attached is not deleted: the API names what it is
attached to. Removing `firewall` from the app or the bucket in the same
configuration is enough when it refers to the firewall by `fpcloud_firewall.<name>.id`,
since the detach is then applied first.

## A change that denies the machine running the apply

A firewall filters requests to the apps and websites it is attached to, and
never the API this provider talks to. A change or an attach that denies the
address the apply runs from is therefore made like any other, and the apply
shows a warning saying so. From a CI runner, which is rarely in an allowlist,
that warning is expected. Nothing has to be set to allow it, and the firewall
can always be changed again from the same machine.

## Edits made outside the configuration

The rules in the configuration are the whole list. An apply writes them over
whatever the firewall holds, including a rule somebody added with the CLI or
in the console since the last apply: the plan shows that rule being removed.

## Rule order and spelling

Rules may be written in any order: `priority` decides the order they are
evaluated in. The API keeps every source as a masked CIDR, so `10.0.0.5` is
stored as `10.0.0.5/32` and `10.1.2.3/8` as `10.0.0.0/8`. Either spelling in the
configuration is the same source and plans no change. An imported firewall is
read the way the API spells it.

## Schema

### Required

- `name` (String) Firewall name, unique in the project. Changing it forces a new firewall.
- `project` (String) ID of the project this firewall belongs to. It attaches to apps and websites of the same project. Changing it forces a new firewall.

### Optional

- `default_action` (String) What happens to a request no enabled rule matches: `allow` or `deny`. Defaults to `allow`, so a firewall with no rules changes nothing. `deny` makes the rules an allowlist.
- `description` (String) What the firewall is for.
- `rules` (Attributes List) The access rules, all of them. A rule is identified by its priority, and rules are evaluated in priority order whatever order they are written in. At most 50 rules and 500 sources across them. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedatt--rules))

### Read-Only

- `created_at` (String) When the firewall was created, RFC 3339.
- `findings` (Attributes List) Warnings about a firewall that is valid and enforced as written: a rule no request can reach, a default of deny with no IPv6 source. Also shown as warnings when an apply writes the firewall. The warning that a change denies the address the apply ran from is shown on that apply only and is not kept here, since it is about the machine and not about the firewall. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedatt--findings))
- `id` (String) Firewall ID. What an app's or a bucket's `firewall` attribute takes.
- `revision` (Number) Counts the firewall's content: every change to the default action or the rules stores the next one. An apply returns once every target enforces it.
- `updated_at` (String) When the firewall last changed, RFC 3339.

<a id="nestedatt--rules"></a>
### Nested Schema for `rules`

Required:

- `action` (String) `allow` or `deny`.
- `match` (Attributes) What the rule matches on. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedatt--rules--match))
- `priority` (Number) Evaluation order, lowest first, between 1 and 65535. Unique within the firewall. Leave gaps so a rule can be added between two others later.

Optional:

- `description` (String) What the rule is for, at most 256 characters.
- `enabled` (Boolean) Whether the rule is evaluated. Defaults to true. A disabled rule is kept and skipped.

<a id="nestedatt--rules--match"></a>
### Nested Schema for `rules.match`

Required:

- `sources` (Set of String) Client address ranges as CIDRs, IPv4 or IPv6; a request from any of them matches. A bare address is the one-address range, so `10.0.0.5` and `10.0.0.5/32` are the same source.



<a id="nestedatt--findings"></a>
### Nested Schema for `findings`

Read-Only:

- `code` (String) What kind of warning it is.
- `field` (String) What it is about, as `rules[2]` or `default_action`; empty when it is about the firewall as a whole.
- `message` (String) The warning.

## Import

Import is supported using the following syntax:

The [`terraform import` command](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/import) can be used, for example:

```shell
# Import by "project/name" (project is the project's id), or by firewall id.
terraform import fpcloud_firewall.office 0d1c7e5a-8b3f-4c2e-9a6d-5f4e3b2a1c0d/office

# Or declaratively (Terraform 1.5+ / OpenTofu):
#   import {
#     to = fpcloud_firewall.office
#     id = "0d1c7e5a-8b3f-4c2e-9a6d-5f4e3b2a1c0d/office"
#   }
```
